sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Akṣobhya** (*akshobhya*) — Immovable, East · The Unshakable, Mirror-Like Wisdom — is the Buddha of the eastern Buddha-field Abhirati and the head of the vajra family in the five-Tathāgata system: the embodiment of a mind that cannot be shaken, and of the mirror-like wisdom that reflects all things exactly as they are.[^1]

His name is a privative compound: *a-kṣobhya*, ‘not to be shaken’, from the root √*kṣubh*, ‘to shake, agitate’ — the Unshakable One. Monier-Williams records the word's double life in Buddhist usage: a name of a Buddha, and a term for an immense number — immovability rendered as countlessness.[^2] The sūtra that tells his origin makes the name a vow kept: as a bodhisattva he resolved never to feel anger or malice toward any being until awakening, and the resolve held — hence the blue, earth-touching Buddha of the east, whose element is the transmutation of anger into wisdom.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Akṣobhya** and serves its temple at [akṣobhya.com](https://xn--akobhya-473c.com). The restoration keeps the retroflex ṣ of the Sanskrit cluster kṣ; the plain ASCII *akshobhya* is a modern convenience of the early domain-name system, not an attested ancient spelling.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (New York: Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Akṣobhya’.
Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. akṣobhya, √kṣubh.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Sanskrit as **अक्षोभ्य** (IAST *akṣobhya*; nominative *akṣobhyaḥ*). It is a privative compound built on the gerundive of √*kṣubh*, ‘to shake, agitate, disturb’: *a-kṣobhya*, ‘not-to-be-shaken, imperturbable, immovable’.[^1] The same lexical family gives the Buddhist counting-term *akṣobhya*, an immense number — the unshakable rendered as the uncountable.[^1]

The name is his biography compressed: the Akṣobhyavyūha tradition tells that as the bodhisattva who would become Akṣobhya he made the vow of patience — never to give rise to anger toward any being — and kept it unbroken to his awakening. ‘Unshakable’ is not a temperament but a kept vow.[^2]

The ASCII form *akshobhya* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling, and it replaces the single retroflex ṣ of the cluster kṣ with the English digraph *sh*. The Unicode restoration **Akṣobhya** recovers the retroflex directly in the address bar. Because the restoration preserves a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses, the name is classified Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **a** → **A** — Same, capitalized
- **k** → **k** — Same
- **s** → **ṣ** — Retroflex ṣ (part of the kṣ cluster)
- **h** → **—** — Dropped (English digraph, not Sanskrit)
- **o** → **o** — Same
- **b** → **b** — Same
- **h** → **h** — Same
- **y** → **y** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

The project holds the domain **akṣobhya.com** (xn--akobhya-473c.com) as the canonical home of this name.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. akṣobhya, √kṣubh.
Akṣobhyavyūha Sūtra (Mahāratnakūṭa collection, T. 310).

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/əˈkʂoː.bʱjə/** — Sanskrit Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **A-** — Short open [ə], the privative prefix *a-*, ‘not, un-’
- **-kṣo-** — The cluster [kʂ], voiceless velar plus retroflex sibilant, with long [oː] (Sanskrit o is always long); the stressed syllable
- **-bhya** — Voiced aspirated bilabial [bʱ] with glide [j] and short [ə]; the gerundive suffix -ya on the root √kṣubh

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: ‘uk-SHOH-bhyuh’ — the ‘sh’ retroflex, tongue curled back; the ‘bh’ one breathy sound.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Sanskrit** — अक्षोभ्य (akṣobhya), ‘the Unshakable’
- **Chinese** — 阿閦佛 (Āchùfó), ‘the Immovable Buddha’
- **Japanese** — Ashuku (Ashuku Nyorai)
- **Tibetan** — Mi bskyod pa (Mikyöpa), ‘the Unshaken’

Akṣobhya is Tier 1 because the retroflex ṣ is a distinctive letter ASCII cannot carry; the digraph ‘sh’ merges two Sanskrit consonants (k + ṣ) into an English guess.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. akṣobhya.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in Devanagari as **अक्षोभ्य** — Brahmic abugida, attested Buddhist Sanskrit, in the sūtra and tantra manuscripts of India and Nepal; the script is written left-to-right.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *Akṣobhya* (IAST), giving the normalized reading /əˈkʂoː.bʱjə/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Akṣobhya is written अक्षोभ्य in Devanagari: अ (a) + क्षो (kṣo) + भ्य (bhya); the conjunct क्ष writes the cluster kṣ — the same ligature that begins [[ksitigarbha|Kṣitigarbha]]'s name.
- The word is a-kṣobhya, the privative of the gerundive of √kṣubh, ‘to shake’: ‘not-to-be-shaken’.
- IAST writes the retroflex sibilant as ṣ (distinguished from palatal ś and dental s).
- The Unicode restoration Akṣobhya is registrable in .com; the Devanagari form is not supported in the .com IDN table.[^2]

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. akṣobhya, √kṣubh.
Edgerton, Franklin, Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit Dictionary (Yale University Press, 1953), s.v. akṣobhya.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Akṣobhya** is the Buddha of the unshakable mind: the easterner of the five Tathāgatas, lord of the vajra family, whose wisdom is the mirror that shows things as they are.[^1]

### Abhirati

His Buddha-field in the east, ‘Delightful’, is one of the earliest pure lands named in Mahāyāna literature — a realm where the vow of patience is the law of the land.[^2]

### Mirror-Like Wisdom

The ādarśa-jñāna: the great mirror wisdom that reflects all phenomena without distortion — the transformed form of anger in the five-wisdom schema.[^1]

### The Vajra Family

He heads the vajra (diamond) clan of the five Buddha-families: blue, eastern, of the element water, with the vajra for his seal.

### The Transmutation of Anger

His psychology is the tradition's answer to hatred: anger not suppressed but seen through, its energy returned as unshakable clarity.

sources.citation: Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1914).
Akṣobhyavyūha Sūtra (Mahāratnakūṭa, T. 310).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography of Akṣobhya is the iconography of firmness:[^1]

- **Bhūmisparśa mudrā** — The earth-touching gesture, right hand to the ground: the seal of [[shakyamuni|Śākyamuni]]'s victory over [[mara|Māra]] becomes Akṣobhya's own, the posture of the unmoved
- **The vajra** — The diamond sceptre, set upon his palm or at his throne: the family emblem of the unbreakable
- **Blue body** — The deep blue of the eastern direction and of water held perfectly still
- **The elephant mount** — In the five-family schema his throne is borne by elephants, the heaviest-footed of animals: weight as a virtue
- **The mirror** — Not held but implied: the ādarśa-jñāna is figured in ritual as the mirror that dirt cannot stain and events cannot startle

sources.citation: Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914), on Akṣobhya and the five Tathāgatas.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Akṣobhya's mythology is the story of a vow kept to the letter.[^1]

### The Vow of Patience (Akṣobhyavyūha Sūtra)

In the Akṣobhyavyūha — preserved as the sixth assembly of the great Mahāratnakūṭa collection — the Buddha tells of a monk of a past age who resolved before an earlier Tathāgata never to give rise to anger or malice toward any being, in any circumstance, until his own awakening. The resolve was kept without a single breach, and on its strength he became the Buddha Akṣobhya, the Unshakable, whose field is Abhirati in the east. The sūtra describes Abhirati as a land where the same patience is native: no anger, no ugliness, no thorn of hatred anywhere in its soil.[^2]

### The Eastern Witness (Prajñāpāramitā and Vimalakīrti)

The early Mahāyāna kept his address current. The Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā knows his eastern field among the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, and the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa makes its hero — the layman whose wisdom shames bodhisattvas — a native of Abhirati who has come to this world on the Buddha Akṣobhya's business: the sharpest lay intellect in the sūtras hails from the Unshakable's land.[^3]

### The Esoteric Enthronement

The tantric systematization of the five Tathāgatas set him at the east of the maṇḍala: head of the vajra family, lord of the mirror-like wisdom, the transmuted form of hatred itself. The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha and its lineages made his blue, earth-touching figure the template for the whole iconography of firmness — and paired the idea with its wrathful mirror, Acala, ‘the Immovable’, whose name glosses the same root resolve.[^4]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Akṣobhya’.
Akṣobhyavyūha Sūtra (Mahāratnakūṭa, T. 310).
Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, trans. Edward Conze (1973); Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, trans. Burton Watson (1997).
Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha; Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Akṣobhya travels under his meaning rather than his sound: Chinese Āchùfó transcribes, but the common understanding is 不動 ‘Immovable’; Japanese Ashuku Nyorai sits east in the esoteric maṇḍalas of Shingon; Tibetan Mi bskyod pa heads the vajra family of the five Jinas.[^1] The system he anchors — five Buddhas as five wisdoms transmuting five poisons — became one of the most portable pieces of Buddhist psychology: anger's energy, unpolluted, is the mirror that sees truly.

Within the PuniCodex cross-tradition index, kindred figures include [[vairocana|Mahāvairocana]] (the centre of the same five-Buddha maṇḍala), [[amitabha|Amitābha]] (the western counterpart in the pentad and the other great pure-land Buddha), and [[vajrapani|Vajrapāṇi]] (the bodhisattva of the same vajra lineage).

sources.citation: Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914).

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Akṣobhya's afterlife is the maṇḍala itself: wherever the five-Buddha schema went — Tang China, Shingon Japan, Tibet, Nepal — his blue earth-touching form held the east. In Japanese esoteric Buddhism he is Ashuku, and his root idea found its most popular mask in Fudō Myōō (Acala), ‘the Immovable One’, whose fiery wrath is the unshakable turned outward to protect.[^1]

His quieter legacy is psychological. The five-wisdom map — anger into mirror-wisdom, pride into equality-wisdom, desire into discernment, envy into accomplishment, ignorance into the wisdom of the dharmadhātu — remains the standard vocabulary of Vajrayana self-understanding, and Akṣobhya's is the conversion most modern practitioners name first: the proof that the tradition never asked anyone to be less intense, only less shaken.[^2]

sources.citation: Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914).
Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Five Buddhas’ and ‘Akṣobhya’.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Akṣobhya is identified in stone and bronze by his signature: the earth-touching right hand and the vajra set before him on the throne. Pāla-period art (8th–12th c.) made him a favourite of the stelae workshops of Bihar and Bengal — the standing and seated blue Buddha of the east appears across the sculpture of Nālandā, Bodhgayā, and Kurkihar — and Nepalese and Tibetan bronzes carried the type across the Himalaya.[^1]

The monumental evidence belongs to the maṇḍala age: the five-Tathāgata crowns and paintings of the Tabo and Alchi temples in the western Himalaya preserve the whole pentad in situ, and the pagodas and lecture halls of Tō-ji in Kyoto keep the Shingon maṇḍala where Ashuku holds the east. The epigraphic anchor for his sūtra's antiquity is its early translation into Chinese within the Mahāratnakūṭa corpus.[^2]

sources.citation: Huntington, Susan L., The ‘Pāla-Sena’ Schools of Sculpture (Leiden: Brill, 1984).
Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Buddhist Art’.

sections.label: Pāli Canon
sections.body:
**Akṣobhya is absent from the Pāli Canon.** The Tipiṭaka nowhere names a Buddha Akṣobhya or a field called Abhirati; as with [[amitabha|Amitābha]], this is a fact of canon and lineage, not a judgement of authenticity. The Pāli tradition closed its canon around teachings traced to the historical Buddha and his first disciples, while the cult of the eastern Tathāgata arose within the Mahāyāna movement and its own claims of authority.[^1]

The Pāli texts do, however, supply the raw virtue he perfects: the Kakacūpama Sutta's simile of the saw (MN 21) — that one should remain unmoved in kindness even if bandits dismember one limb by limb — is the canonical seed of the very patience his vow fulfilled.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Akṣobhya’.
Majjhima Nikāya 21 (Kakacūpama Sutta), trans. Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi (1995).

sections.label: Mahāyāna Sūtras
sections.body:
His charter text is the **Akṣobhyavyūha Sūtra**, transmitted as the sixth assembly of the Mahāratnakūṭa collection (Taishō 310): the vow of patience, the fulfilment, and the description of Abhirati, ‘Delightful’, the eastern field whose ground is free of the dust of anger. It is among the earliest Buddha-field sūtras, older perhaps in its nucleus than the Sukhāvatī texts it parallels.[^1]

The wider sūtra literature keeps his address. The **Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā** ranges his land among the fields of the ten directions; the **Vimalakīrtinirdeśa** makes its hero an emissary of Abhirati — the sharpest wisdom in the lay world native to the Unshakable's realm; and the tantric **Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha** enthrones him in the five-Tathāgata maṇḍala as head of the vajra family, where his mirror-like wisdom becomes system, liturgy, and art.[^2]

sources.citation: Akṣobhyavyūha Sūtra (Mahāratnakūṭa, T. 310).
Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, trans. Conze (1973); Vimalakīrtinirdeśa, trans. Watson (1997); Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha.

sections.label: Commentarial Tradition
sections.body:
India's śāstra literature on Akṣobhya is thin beside the sūtra and tantra record; his interpretation happened mostly inside the five-Buddha system. The tantric commentaries on the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha and the Guhyasamāja cycle fixed the correspondences that define him — east, blue, vajra family, water element, the aggregate of consciousness, the poison hatred transmuted into the mirror-like wisdom — a schema so complete it became the Vajrayana's default psychology.[^1]

East Asian esoteric exegesis, above all the Shingon tradition descending from Kūkai, kept him in ritual memory as Ashuku of the vajra-realm maṇḍala, and Tibetan commentarial tradition made Mi bskyod pa's five-wisdom conversion — hatred into the mirror — a standard teaching of the graduated path.[^2]

sources.citation: Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914).
Hakeda, Yoshito S., trans., Kūkai: Major Works (New York: Columbia University Press, 1972).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Akṣobhya is the Buddha for everyone who has ever been told their anger disqualifies them. His whole biography is one sentence: he resolved not to be moved by hatred, and then was not. The tradition is careful about what this means — not numbness, not suppression, but a mind that events can no longer push around, a mirror that the fiercest fire passes over without dimming.

The mirror is the perfect emblem: a mirror does not fight what it reflects and does not flinch from it; it simply shows. His question to a stirred mind is the gentlest in the maṇḍala: what, exactly, is shaking you — and what would you see if it stopped?

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Akṣobhya’.
